scenario: You c-bet A♠K♣ on Q♦7♠2♣ (flop), one caller. Turn K♥ — you now have top pair top kicker.
question: You improved to TPTK on the turn. Plan?
explanation: Hardin's turn criteria #1: 'we have a value hand worth betting.' You turned TPTK — bet for value. Betting the turn is crucial to building the pot for a larger river bet. Any card that improves your hand to a stronger value hand is a barrel candidate. Double barrel for value — you have a value hand worth betting, and the K improved you; build the pot.

scenario: You semi-bluff c-bet J♠T♠ on 9♠6♦2♣ (flop) with a flush draw + overcards, one caller. Turn 8♥ — you pick up an open-ended straight draw too (now OESD + flush draw).
question: Turn gave you a monster combo draw. Barrel?
options: Check — you still have nothing made
explanation: Hardin's turn criteria #2: 'we pick up turn barreling equity.' You now have ~15 outs (9 flush + 6 straight, minus overlap) AND fold equity. Combo draws this strong are mandatory double barrels — you have huge equity when called and fold equity when not. The backdoor-becomes-draw turn is the classic barrel card. Double barrel semi-bluff — you picked up barreling equity (flush + straight draws = ~15 outs) plus fold equity.

scenario: You c-bet K♣Q♦ on 8♠5♦3♥ (flop), one caller. Turn 2♣ (total blank, didn't help you). You have two overcards, no draw. Opponent folds to turn c-bets only 30% of the time.
question: Blank turn, no equity gained, sticky opponent. Barrel again?
explanation: None of Hardin's four barrel criteria are met: no value hand, no barreling equity gained, opponent doesn't fold enough (30%), and no scare card hit your range. Firing a second barrel here is spew. Check and give up — you'll often still see a free showdown or fold the river. Knowing when to STOP barreling is as important as when to start. No — you have no value, no equity gain, and low fold equity (30% fold to turn cbet).

scenario: YOUR HAND. You called a 3-bet with K♠T♠ on Q-J-6. Villain bets flop, you call. Turn blank, villain bets again, you call. River blank, villain fires a THIRD barrel (near pot).
question: Villain triple-barrels into you. You have K-high (the gutshot bricked). Action?
explanation: Your real hand (−97 BB). When a tight player fires all three streets ('empties the clip') at micro stakes, it's almost never a bluff — their range is strong made hands that beat your busted K-high. You picked up nothing. The whole hand was a lesson in this: each call compounded the leak. Fold to the triple barrel — believe the story their betting tells. Fold — a TAG emptying the clip (3 barrels) on Q-J-6-x-x has a value range (QQ+/sets/AK-made) that you never beat with K-high; micro players don't triple-barrel bluff.

scenario: You c-bet A♥9♦ on 9♣6♠2♦ (top pair), one caller. Turn K♠ (overcard to your pair). Opponent is a TAG who called the flop.
question: You have middle-strength top pair (9s), turn brings an overcard K. Barrel again?
explanation: Your double-barrel rate (65%) runs high, and this is the kind of turn to check. The K is a scare card that hits the caller's flop-calling range (any Kx, KJ/KQ floats) more than yours. Barreling here bets into the exact card that improved them, and your pair of nines is only medium strength. Check for pot control. Knowing which turns to SHUT DOWN on is the other half of barreling. The K is a scare card that hits the CALLER's range (Kx that floated), not yours; your 9s is now medium and vulnerable. Pot-control, don't barrel into the card that helped them.

scenario: You c-bet Q♠Q♦ on 8♦5♣2♠ (overpair), one caller. Turn 7♥ (mostly blank). TAG opponent, folds to turn cbet ~55%.
question: Overpair QQ on a dry-ish board, blank turn, opponent folds to turn barrels often. Plan?
explanation: This IS a barrel — and shows barreling isn't always wrong. Hardin criteria: you have a value hand worth betting (QQ overpair, dry board with little that beat you), and the opponent folds to turn cbets 55% (good fold equity). Bet for value and denial. The skill is distinguishing THIS (strong value, dry board, foldy opponent) from the previous spot (medium hand, scare card, sticky opponent). Same action, opposite reasoning — read the factors. Double barrel for value + denial — QQ is a strong value hand worth betting, the board is dry (low straight/flush risk), and the opponent over-folds turns; bet to extract from worse and deny equity.

scenario: You raised preflop and c-bet A♥K♥ on J♠7♦2♣, one caller. Turn 9♥ completes a backdoor-ish heart texture that connects far more with YOUR suited-broadway raising range than with a capped BB calling range. You still have just ace-high with a flush draw now.
question: The turn card favors your range more than theirs, even though you personally just picked up a draw. Barrel again?
options: Bet — the card favors your range
Give up, too scary a river coming
explanation: A scare card is only scary for the player whose range it doesn't fit. Here the new heart favors YOUR raising range (suited broadways) more than BB's capped flatting range, on top of which you also picked up a flush draw of your own. Both the range-based scare-card criterion and the equity-gain criterion point the same way. Double barrel — the turn card hits your range harder than theirs, and you also picked up real equity; this is a clean semi-bluff, not a coinflip.

scenario: You c-bet 8♠8♦ on K♣8♥3♣, flopping a set, one caller. Turn 6♦ (blank). Opponent is a loose-passive calling station who rarely folds once they've called a flop bet.
question: You have a set, the caller is sticky, the turn is a total blank. Does low fold equity change anything?
options: Check — you have no fold equity to lean on
Bet — pure value, folds don't matter
explanation: Fold equity only matters for bluffs — a made hand this strong doesn't need anyone to fold. A set on a dry-ish board against a station who calls with worse pairs and kings is a value bet regardless of what their fold-to-turn-cbet number says. Hardin's criterion #1 (a value hand worth betting) is met on its own; you don't need the other three. Bet for value — a set doesn't care about fold equity; a station who never folds is exactly who you want to keep betting into.

scenario: You c-bet A♣K♦ on A♠8♠3♥, top pair top kicker, one caller. Turn 8♦ pairs the board. This caller's preflop range (a BB defend vs your CO open) is wide but very light on random 8x combos.
question: The turn pairs the board — does that automatically make barreling dangerous?
options: Check — any paired turn is risky
Check unless you have the case card
Bet — wide range rarely holds it
Bet half pot to be safe
explanation: A paired board only threatens you if the opponent's continuing range actually contains that rank in real volume. A wide BB-defense range is built from suited connectors, broadways, and small-to-mid pairs, not a heavy concentration of exactly one specific rank like 8x — and pairing the board also removes combos of it from the deck. Your TPTK barely loses value here. Double barrel for value — a paired turn is often safe to barrel into a wide, unselective range, since that range rarely holds the exact card that paired in real numbers.

scenario: You c-bet K♠K♥ on Q♦7♣2♠, one caller, effective stacks still 3x the pot after the flop bet. Turn 4♥ (blank).
question: You have a big value hand and stacks are deep enough for a third barrel to matter. Does planning ahead change your turn sizing?
options: Shove the entire stack right now instead
Bet — size with the river in mind
explanation: With a real value hand and real stack depth left, the turn bet isn't just about this street — it's setting up the river. Sizing the turn so a pot-sized (or larger) river bet still fits the remaining stack keeps your triple-barrel line coherent and threatening, rather than either under-betting and running out of room, or overbetting the turn and leaving an awkward river. Bet the turn with the river in mind — good barreling plans the whole hand's sizing, not just the current street.

scenario: You c-bet Q♠J♠ on T♠4♦2♠ (flush draw + gutshot), one caller. Turn 8♠ completes your flush outright — you now hold the nuts.
question: You just made the nut flush. Bet big or small?
options: Bet small to keep them in
explanation: Once you have the actual nuts on a board with a live flush possibility, the priority flips from 'induce action cheaply' to 'get paid before the scare factor keeps them from calling at all.' A big bet here still gets called by any made hand or draw the caller has, and there's no future street where this is more +EV to check back. Bet big — with the nuts made, extract now rather than trying to be cute; the hand only gets harder to get paid on from here.

scenario: You 3-bet from the BB, BTN calls. You c-bet A♦T♣ on K♥7♣3♦, missed entirely. Turn is A♠ — you now have top pair, and this is exactly the kind of card that BTN's capped calling range (already missing most premium Ax after facing your 3-bet) doesn't hold.
question: 3-bet pot, the turn ace both gives you a pair AND is a card BTN's range is light on. Barrel?
options: Check — an ace on board is always scary
Check, should've given up on flop
explanation: This combines two criteria at once: you now have a real, if thin, value hand (top pair), and the specific card favors YOUR continuing range in a 3-bet pot (most weak aces already folded to your 3-bet preflop, so BTN's calling range was never full of aces to begin with). Double barrel — you both improved and picked a card that BTN's range doesn't want to see; this is a strong combined spot, not a coin flip.

scenario: You c-bet 9♣9♦ on 9♠5♥2♣ (flopped a set), one caller. Turn 7♠ (mostly blank). This is a 3-way pot — one more caller besides you and the original flop-caller — wait: two other players also called your flop bet, so it's now three-way going to the turn.
question: You have a set in a three-way pot. Does the extra opponent change whether you should keep betting?
options: Bet only a small, token-sized amount here
Bet — a real hand still bets multiway
Bet vs only one of the two
explanation: Multiway caution is about vulnerable one-pair hands, not about strong made hands. A flopped set on a dry-ish, unpaired board is still well ahead of two full ranges' worth of continuing hands, and more opponents in the pot is actually more potential value, not more danger, when your hand is this far ahead. Bet for value — a real hand like a set doesn't get weaker just because more people are watching; the multiway caution is for overpairs and top pair, not sets.

scenario: You raised BTN, BB called. You checked back the flop (6♦4♣2♥, total whiff) planning a delayed c-bet. Turn J♥ gives you a backdoor gutshot-ish overcard pair candidate — actually you now hold two overcards to a paired-nothing board plus a running gutshot possibility. BB checks again.
question: You checked the flop planning to attack later. BB checks turn too — does this change anything?
options: Check — already gave up on flop
Never bet after checking a flop
Bet only with a made hand
explanation: Checking back the flop wasn't giving up — it was a delayed c-bet plan, and BB's second consecutive check is real information: their range likely missed the flop too and still hasn't improved. This is exactly the spot a delayed c-bet is designed for. Bet the turn — two checks from BB signals a weak, giving-up range; this is the moment the delayed plan pays off, not a reason to check a third time.

scenario: You c-bet A♣Q♣ on K♦9♦4♥, missed, one caller with a fold-to-turn-cbet of 74%. Turn 2♠ (total blank, changes nothing).
question: You still have zero equity, but the opponent folds to turn c-bets 74% of the time. Barrel anyway?
options: Bet — high fold rate alone is enough
Check — zero equity always means you check
Bet the river only, not the turn
explanation: Hardin's four criteria don't all need to be present at once — a strong enough read on any single one can be enough by itself. A 74% fold-to-turn-cbet rate means three times out of four this bet just wins the pot outright, which comfortably justifies firing with air. Bet as a pure bluff — an extreme fold-to-cbet stat can carry a barrel on its own, even with zero added equity; compare this to a sticky opponent, where the same air hand should just check.

scenario: You c-bet K♣J♣ on Q♠T♦4♣ (gutshot + overcard + backdoor flush), one caller. Turn 9♣ completes both your straight draw into a made hand AND your flush draw into a made flush — you now have the nut straight flush... no, correction: you now hold the nut flush (K♣J♣ with three clubs out).
question: You went from a combo draw to the nut flush on the turn. How does your plan change?
options: Bet — same action, now for value
Check, you already had fold equity
Keep the flop-sized bet, no change
explanation: The bet stays the same (bet), but the reason behind it flips entirely — you're no longer betting for fold equity plus backup outs, you're betting because you now have the best possible hand. Recognizing that shift matters for sizing (go bigger, you want value, not just folds) and for how you react to a raise (you're now likely ahead, not just semi-bluffing). Bet, now for value — the action doesn't change, but the reasoning and correct sizing do, once a draw actually completes into the nuts.

scenario: You c-bet A♠9♠ on 9♦6♠3♠ (top pair, backdoor flush draw), one caller. Turn 5♠ completes your flush — you hold the nut flush now, and this card also looks scary to any Kx/Qx-type hand the caller might have floated with.
question: You made the nuts AND the card looks scary to their likely floats. Does that change sizing from a normal value bet?
options: Min-bet just to guarantee you get a call
explanation: A card being scary to a float range mostly matters for BLUFFS (more fold equity) — it doesn't change how much a made hand should bet for value against the part of their range that does continue (pairs, better draws before this card, or a slower-played big hand). Treat this as a normal value bet with the nuts: size for what a calling range will pay, not smaller just because some of their range folds anyway. Bet a normal value size — the scare-card effect helps bluffs get folds; it doesn't mean you should shrink a genuine value bet with the nuts.

scenario: You c-bet T♥T♦ on 9♠5♦2♣ (overpair), one caller. Turn 9♥ pairs the board — but you hold no 9 and the caller is a wide, unselective calling station who defends with almost anything.
question: The turn pairs a card you don't hold, against a caller wide enough to sometimes have that exact card. Bet or check?
options: Check — too risky vs a wide range
explanation: Yes, a truly wide, unselective range is more likely than a narrow one to contain the odd 9x combo — but 'more likely' doesn't mean 'usually.' The overwhelming majority of a wide calling range is still worse pairs, ace-high, and busted draws, all of which TT still beats even after the board pairs. Bet for value — a wide station range is bad news in raw frequency of trips compared to a tight range, but it's still mostly worse hands; don't let one bad-case scenario override the math.

scenario: You c-bet A♦K♠ on K♦9♣4♦, top pair top kicker, one caller. Turn 3♦ brings a third diamond to the board — you hold the A♦, blocking the nut flush.
question: A flush just became possible and you hold the ace of the flush suit. Does that blocker support continuing to bet?
options: Check — a third suited card, always
Check unless you also pair that suit
explanation: A flush becoming possible doesn't mean you're facing one — it means you should account for how likely it actually is, and holding the nut card of that suit directly lowers that likelihood while also meaning that if you're ever raised, it's less likely to be the flush specifically. Betting still charges the large part of their range that doesn't have three diamonds. Bet for value/protection — the nut blocker both reduces the flush's likelihood and improves your position if you do get raised; this is a reason to keep betting, not to slow down.

scenario: You raised BTN, BB called — you are in position. You c-bet J♦T♦ on 9♠8♦2♣ (gutshot + backdoor flush + two overcards worth of range advantage), one caller. Turn 7♦ gives you an open-ended straight draw plus your flush draw is now also live.
question: In position, you picked up a monster combo draw on the turn. Bet, or check back to control the pot since you're IP?
options: Check back, take the free card
Bet — equity beats a free card
Check back, then raise if bet into
explanation: Being in position gives you the OPTION to check back profitably — it doesn't mean checking is always better. With an open-ended straight draw and a flush draw combined (a huge number of outs) plus real fold equity on top, betting captures value a free card can't: it wins the pot outright a good chunk of the time, and builds a pot for when you do complete. Bet — a monster combo draw is a bet, not a check, in position or not; the free-card option is only worth taking when there isn't this much to gain from betting.

scenario: You c-bet A♣J♦ on Q♠8♥3♣, missed, one caller with a fold-to-turn-cbet of only 18%. Turn 6♦ (blank, changes nothing).
question: You have zero equity and the opponent almost never folds a turn c-bet. Fire again anyway?
options: Bet an even bigger overbet than usual
Check — fold rate too low to bluff
explanation: None of Hardin's four criteria are met: no value hand, no new equity, a blank turn (no favorable scare card), and — the clincher — an 18% fold-to-turn-cbet rate means this bet gets called or raised over four times out of five. A pure bluff with a stat this bad is just burning money. Check and give up — an extremely low fold-to-turn-cbet rate is disqualifying on its own for a zero-equity bluff, regardless of anything else about the hand.

scenario: You c-bet A♠A♦ on J♦9♦4♣ (overpair, no diamond), one caller who floated the flop with a wide range including a lot of diamond draws. Turn 2♦ completes a third diamond.
question: The turn card is exactly the suit your caller was likely drawing to, and you hold none of it. Barrel your overpair?
options: Bet small to see where you're at
Bet, then auto-fold to a raise
explanation: This is the textbook 'barreling into the card that helped them' mistake. If you know their flop-calling range was diamond-heavy, the third diamond is the single worst turn card for your overpair, and you hold no blocker to soften it. AA is still a real hand, but this specific card should trigger a pot-control check, not a continued bet. Check — a scare card that specifically fits the range you're facing is exactly when to slow down, even with a big pocket pair.

scenario: You c-bet K♥Q♠ on K♦7♣2♥ (top pair, weak-ish kicker for the situation), one caller, but this pot is three-way — two other players also called your flop bet. Turn 9♠ (blank).
question: Top pair, no kicker help, and now three-way. Keep betting for value/protection?
options: Bet bigger to fold out both
explanation: This is the flip side of the earlier set example — a genuinely big hand (a set) can still bet multiway, but a merely decent hand like top pair with a so-so kicker gets much more dangerous the more live ranges are behind it. Two callers combined are far more likely to have two pair, a set, or a better kicker than one caller alone. Check or bet small with a give-up plan — multiway pots need real strength to keep firing; top pair alone often isn't enough against two live opponents.

scenario: You c-bet A♥K♥ on K♠9♦4♣ (top pair top kicker), one caller. Turn 9♣ pairs the board (unrelated to your hand). You have decent showdown value already, and betting a polarized range here would mean folding out worse kings while only getting called by 9x/better.
question: You have real showdown value, but betting mostly folds out worse and gets called by better. What's the better plan?
options: Bet big to protect vs trips
Bet small to induce a raise
Bet, then fold to any raise
explanation: This is the 'polarization' trap — a hand with real but not overwhelming showdown value often does worse by betting than by checking, when a bet's likely responses are 'fold something worse' or 'call/raise with something better.' Checking lets you realize the showdown value you already have without paying to find out you're behind. Check — TPTK with genuine showdown value doesn't need to bet a paired, mostly-irrelevant turn; let the hand play itself out cheaply instead.

scenario: You c-bet A♦Q♦ on Q♣8♠5♦ (top pair top kicker), and the caller check-raised your flop c-bet — you called the check-raise. Turn 2♠ (blank).
question: You called a flop check-raise (a strong action from most players) and now face a decision on the turn. Lead out again?
options: Bet big to find out where you stand
explanation: A check-raise is one of the strongest signals in poker — most players don't check-raise as a pure bluff nearly as often as they do it for value or a strong draw. Calling it was reasonable with TPTK, but leading out again on the turn ignores the information you already paid to see. Check — a flop check-raise already told you a lot; let them act first on the turn rather than betting into a range that already showed strength.

scenario: Effective stacks are very deep (250bb+). You c-bet Q♣J♣ on J♠8♦3♣ (top pair, no draw beyond the pair itself), one caller. Turn 5♥ (blank, no new equity, no scare card for either range).
question: Deep stacks, no new equity gained, a blank that doesn't especially favor either range. Barrel again?
explanation: Stack depth doesn't create a reason to barrel on its own — it just raises the stakes of the decision you'd otherwise make. Nothing changed here: no new equity, no favorable card, no read given on fold-to-turn-cbet. Firing into a deep stack with only a middling top pair on a static board is how a small mistake turns into an expensive one. Check for pot control — deep stacks are a reason to be MORE careful with a marginal hand, not a blanket reason to keep betting.

scenario: You c-bet 7♣6♣ on 9♦5♣2♥ (open-ended straight draw, no pair), one caller. Turn K♠ bricks your draw completely (no new outs, and it's an overcard that doesn't help your hand at all).
question: Your draw missed, the turn is a total brick for your hand, and you have nothing. Bet as a pure bluff?
options: Check — no real basis to bluff
Bet big, it's now or never
explanation: A card 'looking scary' in the abstract isn't a reason to bluff by itself — you need an actual basis for believing it works (a range read, a fold-to-cbet stat, or genuine leftover equity), none of which are present here. Betting just because a king showed up, with no supporting read, is hoping rather than reasoning. Check and give up — 'it looks like a scare card' isn't one of Hardin's real criteria; without a fold-equity read or backup equity, this bluff has no actual basis.

scenario: You c-bet A♠K♣ on K♦8♠4♥ (top pair top kicker), one caller you've specifically noted 'never folds any pair, ever' in past hands. Turn 2♣ (blank).
question: You have a real value hand, but does 'they never fold a pair' change how you think about a check here versus a normal opponent?
options: Bet — sticky reads support value bets
Check, but only due to the blank
explanation: It's worth pausing on this one: a 'never folds a pair' read is actually a reason TO bet, not to check — it means worse pairs and worse kickers will pay you off, which is exactly what a value bet wants. The trap would be thinking 'they never fold, so betting accomplishes nothing' — that logic applies to bluffs (no fold equity), not to value bets (which don't need folds to profit). Bet for value — a sticky opponent who never folds a pair is a green light for betting a genuine hand, not a reason to check; don't confuse the bluffing logic with the value-betting logic.

scenario: You raised UTG, BB called — you are out of position for the rest of the hand. You c-bet K♠Q♠ on Q♥9♣4♠ (top pair, decent kicker), one caller who has raised your turn bets in two prior hands you remember, both times with the actual best hand. Turn 6♥ (blank).
question: Out of position, facing a caller who's shown they raise turns for real value, with only a decent (not great) top pair. Bet again?
options: Bet — a decent kicker is enough
Bet bigger to fold them out
Check — OOP vs a proven value-raiser
explanation: Being out of position means a raise is more costly to deal with — you can't just check back and control the river the way you could in position. Combined with a specific, credible read that this player raises turns with real hands (not speculatively), betting a good-but-not-great top pair into that exact pattern is asking to face a decision you don't want. Check — OOP against a player who's shown they raise for value, a merely-good hand should take the free card and reassess on the river instead of bet-folding into a bad spot.

scenario: You c-bet A♦4♦ on K♣9♦5♦ (backdoor flush draw only, no pair, no real draw yet beyond two diamonds), one caller. Turn 2♠ bricks completely — no diamond, no pair, no straight card, nothing.
question: A backdoor draw that never materialized, a total brick turn, and no pair. Fire a second bluff barrel?
options: Bet bigger to make up for it
Call if they lead the river instead
Check — sunk cost, no new basis
explanation: Having already bet the flop isn't a reason to keep betting the turn — that's sunk-cost thinking, not a real barrel criterion. The backdoor flush draw needed running diamonds and didn't get help on the turn, leaving you with nothing: no value, no equity, and (absent a specific fold-equity read) no clear basis to keep firing. Check and give up — money already put in the pot doesn't justify more; evaluate the turn barrel decision fresh, based on what's true now, not on what you already bet.
